m1.quote: That's not disqualifying for an OSS project, but it means the "enterprise-grade" framing (audit logs, personas, OAuth broker, compliance-oriented tables) is being asserted by the same small team that built it, with no named third-party validation of production use at scale.
m1.note: Ties the single-maintainer/small-team status to absent external scrutiny and audit of security-critical (OAuth) code, going beyond a pure bus-factor concern.

m2.quote: Building your own OAuth 2.1 authorization server (with DCR, redirect_uri validation, PKCE) is one of the highest-risk things a project can do — this is exactly the kind of code where subtle bugs turn into account takeover or token leakage, and it's an area the industry generally recommends *not* reimplementing unless absolutely necessary.
m2.note: Explicitly frames the built-in authorization server as hand-rolled auth and a red flag, invoking the don't-reimplement-auth norm.

m3.note: It engages directly with the benchmark and DOI report, criticizing it as self-graded and single-model rather than claiming evidence is absent.

m4.note: It correctly reports the PostgreSQL-only path and only says the headline cross-enrichment feature needs a DataHub-centric stack, which is the permitted carve-out.
